introduction-the-gpu-is-a-hungry-mouth.core: A GPU can consume gigabytes of training data per second. If storage, network or decoding can't keep up, the expensive GPU idles waiting on I/O, so AI storage is designed for throughput and parallelism first.

first_principles.problem: GPU utilisation sits at 40% because data loading takes longer than each training step.
truths: Compute has outpaced storage bandwidth.
Idle GPUs waste money.
Data pipelines have several stages that can bottleneck.
derivation: **Prefetch** and cache close to the GPU.

analogy.title: A Formula 1 pit crew waiting for the car
analogy.story: The crew is world-class, but useless if the car isn't there.
analogy.breaks: A pit crew works in bursts; a GPU wants a continuous stream.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Profile I/O before buying more GPUs.

check.q: What's the first metric to check when GPU utilisation is low?
check.a: Time spent waiting on the data loader per step versus compute time.

parallel-filesystems-lustre-gpfs.core: Parallel filesystems like Lustre and GPFS (Spectrum Scale) stripe each file across many storage servers, so thousands of clients read in parallel at aggregate bandwidths of hundreds of GB/s. A separate metadata server handles namespace operations.

first_principles.problem: An NFS server tops out at ~1 GB/s while 256 GPUs need far more.
truths: One server has a bandwidth ceiling.
Striping spreads load across servers.
Metadata and data have different access patterns.

analogy.title: A multi-lane motorway instead of a single-lane road
analogy.story: Traffic spreads across many lanes, so throughput scales with lanes.
analogy.breaks: The metadata server is a single booth, so millions of tiny files still create a jam.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each shard read from 16 servers at once.

check.q: Why do parallel filesystems struggle with millions of tiny files?
check.a: Every open and stat hits the metadata server, which becomes the bottleneck regardless of data bandwidth.

object-storage-the-data-lake.core: Object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) stores immutable objects in a flat namespace accessed over HTTP. It is cheap, durable and effectively infinite, but has per-request latency and no POSIX semantics, so it rewards large sequential reads.

first_principles.problem: Petabytes of training data need a cheap, durable home accessible from any cluster.
truths: HTTP requests have fixed overhead (~10–100 ms).
Objects are immutable, written whole.
Throughput scales with parallel requests.

analogy.title: An enormous warehouse with a counter service
analogy.story: You can't wander the aisles; you ask for a box by label and it's handed over, so it's best to order big boxes.
analogy.breaks: A warehouse can't serve a thousand people at once, but object stores scale with parallel requests.

example.title: Parallel shard download

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Saturates the NIC instead of crawling one file at a time.

code.text:
aws configure set default.s3.max_concurrent_requests 64
aws s3 cp s3://datasets/train/ /nvme/train/ --recursive

example.outcome: data lake throughput scaled with parallelism.

check.q: Why are big objects better than small ones in S3?
check.a: Each request carries fixed latency, so fewer, larger requests amortise overhead and give higher throughput.

the-fast-path-gpudirect-storage-gds.core: Normally data travels disk → CPU RAM (bounce buffer) → GPU memory, which costs CPU cycles and memory bandwidth. GPUDirect Storage uses DMA to move data straight from NVMe or the network into GPU memory, cutting latency and freeing the CPU.

first_principles.problem: Data-loading CPU threads are saturated copying buffers, and throughput plateaus.
truths: Each copy costs bandwidth and CPU.
PCIe allows peer-to-peer DMA.
The GPU is the final destination anyway.
derivation: **DMA** from NVMe/NIC to GPU memory (cuFile API).

analogy.title: Delivering straight to the kitchen instead of via the front desk
analogy.story: The parcel no longer stops at reception to be carried upstairs.
analogy.breaks: It only works if the building layout allows it, i.e. the PCIe topology must support peer-to-peer.

example.title: Before and after GDS
flow: Bounce path: 6 GB/s, 8 CPU cores busy
example.outcome: faster loading with a freed CPU.

check.a: The intermediate copy through CPU system memory (the bounce buffer).

the-small-file-problem-the-inode-killer.core: Datasets like ImageNet hold millions of ~100 KB files. Every file needs metadata operations (open, stat, close) and its own request, so per-file overhead, not bandwidth, dominates, crushing metadata servers and object-store request rates.

first_principles.problem: Reading 1.2M small JPEGs per epoch generates millions of metadata ops and the loader crawls.
truths: Per-file overhead is fixed regardless of size.
Metadata servers have limited ops/s.
Random small reads defeat disk and network efficiency.
derivation: Compute **ops/s needed** = files per epoch ÷ epoch time.

analogy.title: Posting a million postcards instead of one parcel
analogy.story: Each postcard needs its own stamp, sorting and delivery, and the post office drowns.
analogy.breaks: The post office scales with staff, but a single metadata server doesn't scale horizontally.

check.q: Why doesn't faster disk fix the small-file problem?
check.a: The limit is per-file metadata operations and request overhead, not byte throughput.

solving-small-files-aggregation-tartfrec.core: Pack many small samples into large shard files (TAR for WebDataset, TFRecord, Parquet, or MosaicML MDS) of roughly 100 MB–1 GB. Loaders then stream big sequential reads and shuffle within and across shards.

first_principles.problem: Millions of tiny files overwhelm metadata and request rates.
truths: Sequential reads of large files are efficient.
Shuffling can happen at the shard and buffer level.
Formats can hold samples plus labels together.
derivation: **Shuffle** shard order plus an in-memory buffer.
**Index** shards for random access when needed.

analogy.title: Shipping containers instead of loose boxes
analogy.story: Loading one container moves thousands of items in a single crane lift.
analogy.breaks: You can't easily pull one item from a sealed container; shards need an index for random access.

example.title: WebDataset loading

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 1,024 big reads instead of 1.28M small ones.

example.outcome: loader throughput limited only by bandwidth.

points: Pick a format for your data.

check.q: How do you keep randomness when reading sequential shards?
check.a: Shuffle shard order each epoch and use an in-memory shuffle buffer across samples.

streaming-architecture-training-without-.core: Instead of copying a whole dataset to local disk before training, stream shards from object storage on demand with prefetching and a local cache. Training starts immediately, local disk can be smaller than the dataset, and multiple nodes coordinate which shards they read.

first_principles.problem: A 50 TB dataset takes hours to download, and nodes don't have 50 TB of local disk.
truths: Training reads data sequentially per epoch.
Prefetching can hide network latency.
Nodes must not duplicate work in distributed training.

analogy.title: Streaming a film instead of downloading it
analogy.story: You start watching in seconds while the next minutes buffer in the background.
analogy.breaks: Films play once linearly; training needs shuffling and exact resumption, which streaming libraries must add.

example.title: MosaicML Streaming

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Training starts in minutes; each rank reads its own shards.

code.text:
from streaming import StreamingDataset
ds = StreamingDataset(remote='s3://bucket/mds', local='/nvme/cache', shuffle=True)

example.outcome: dataset size decoupled from local disk.

check.q: What must a streaming loader handle in distributed training?
check.a: Assigning disjoint shards to each rank and worker, and resuming deterministically after interruption.
